The Socialist Party USA. Founded in 1901 and formally established under that name in 1973, it advocated for democratic socialism, workers' rights, and labor self-management.

The party emerged from a merger of the Socialist Labor Party and the Social Democratic Party, consolidating radical labor activists, Marxist intellectuals, and immigrant workers—particularly Germans and Eastern Europeans. Eugene V. Debs, a railroad labor organizer, became the party's most prominent figure. He ran as the presidential candidate five times between 1900 and 1920. His 1912 campaign was the party's peak: Debs netted 6 percent of the popular vote, the highest socialist showing in U.S. history.

The party advocated for workers' ownership of the means of production, abolition of the wage system, massive redistribution of wealth, and workers' democratic control of industry. Beyond the presidency, Socialists achieved institutional power. Emil Seidel was elected mayor of Milwaukee in 1910, and the party elected state legislators in the early twentieth century, particularly in the upper Midwest and parts of New York.

But internal divisions weakened the movement. After the 1917 Russian Revolution, democratic socialists and communists increasingly disagreed over ideology and tactics. Many revolutionary members departed for the Communist Party by the 1920s. And after World War II, Cold War anticommunism suppressed radical politics more broadly. The New Deal, meanwhile, incorporated labor protections, unemployment insurance, and welfare measures that Socialists had championed, draining away much of their constituency.

The party's decline accelerated through the mid-twentieth century, though it persisted as a significant early twentieth-century third party rooted in class politics.
